---
title: "Field guide: context and memory"
description: "What a model can see now, and what a system can make available later"
---

A model does not automatically remember a previous call. This page separates the material included in the current request from the systems that store and retrieve material for later requests.

:::

<div class="concept-contrast"><div><strong>Context window</strong>Everything available to the model during this inference call.</div><div><strong>Memory system</strong>Code that stores something and decides whether to put it into a later context window.</div></div>

## Context window {#context-window}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Week 3</span>

**In plain English.** The context window is the maximum token capacity available for the current inference call. It contains input tokens and must also leave room for the generated output.

```python
context_capacity = 1000
input_tokens = 760
reserved_output_tokens = 200
unused_tokens = context_capacity - input_tokens - reserved_output_tokens
print(unused_tokens)
```

<div class="glossary-output">40</div>

**Input → operation → output.** Three integers represent a simplified token budget. Subtraction shows the remaining capacity.

**Why it matters.** “The model supports a long context” does not tell us which sources were included, where they appeared or how much output space remained.

## Input and output token budgets {#token-budget}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Week 3</span>

**In plain English.** The input budget covers instructions, source material and conversation history. The output budget limits the continuation generated by the model.

```python
budget = {"input": 760, "output_limit": 200}
print("Planned total:", budget["input"] + budget["output_limit"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">Planned total: 960</div>

**Common confusion.** The output limit is a ceiling, not a promise that the model will generate exactly that many tokens.

## Truncation {#truncation}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Week 3</span>

**In plain English.** Truncation removes material because it does not fit or because the program deliberately shortens it.

```python
excerpts = ["opening", "case A", "case B", "counterexample", "conclusion"]
visible_excerpts = excerpts[-3:]
print(visible_excerpts)
```

<div class="glossary-output">['case B', 'counterexample', 'conclusion']</div>

**Input → operation → output.** `[-3:]` keeps only the final three items. The removed items do not become invisible in a mysterious way; this Python operation excludes them before the request.

**Why it matters.** A model cannot consider evidence that the program did not send. Save the inclusion and exclusion rule.

## Stateless calls and conversation history {#stateless-history}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 3 and 6</span>

**In plain English.** A basic model endpoint is stateless: it responds to the current request. A continuing conversation works because the program sends earlier turns again or retrieves a stored state.

```python
history = [{"role": "user", "content": "Tell me about the rent increase."}]
history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": "What changed first?"})
history.append({"role": "user", "content": "We began sharing groceries."})
print(len(history))
```

<div class="glossary-output">3</div>

**Input → operation → output.** `.append(...)` mutates the list by adding each turn. A later call can see those turns only if `history` is included in its messages.

**Why it matters.** Saving the realized history shows exactly which earlier questions and answers could influence a later model turn.

## Attention and long context {#attention-long-context}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Week 3</span>

**In plain English.** Attention is part of the model computation that relates token representations to one another. A passage being inside the context window does not guarantee that it will influence the return equally.

```python
passages = {
    "opening": {"included": True, "checked_in_answer": False},
    "counterexample": {"included": True, "checked_in_answer": True},
}
print(passages["opening"])
```

<div class="glossary-output">{'included': True, 'checked_in_answer': False}</div>

**Why it matters.** Inclusion and use are different empirical questions. Source checks should test whether the answer actually reflects relevant passages, especially material buried inside a long prompt.

See Liu et al.'s “Lost in the Middle” study for evidence that model performance can depend on where information appears in a long context.

## External memory {#external-memory}

<span class="term-meta">Core · Weeks 3 and 11</span>

**In plain English.** External memory is stored information outside the model weights that a surrounding program may place into a future request.

```python
memory = []
memory.append({"participant": "T01", "note": "Help preceded meeting attendance."})
retrieved_note = memory[0]["note"]
print(retrieved_note)
```

<div class="glossary-output">Help preceded meeting attendance.</div>

**Input → operation → output.** A dictionary is stored in a list and later retrieved. The list is memory only because the program preserves and reuses it.

**Common confusion.** Memory is not the same as a context window. Retrieved memory becomes useful to the model only when it is inserted into a new request.

## Embeddings {#embeddings}

<span class="term-meta advanced">Advanced · Weeks 3 and 11</span>

**In plain English.** An embedding is a list of numbers representing an item in a space where some forms of similarity can be calculated.

```python
passage_embedding = [0.12, -0.44, 0.81]
query_embedding = [0.08, -0.40, 0.76]
paired_values = list(zip(passage_embedding, query_embedding))
print(paired_values)
```

<div class="glossary-output">[(0.12, 0.08), (-0.44, -0.4), (0.81, 0.76)]</div>

**Why it matters.** Embedding similarity is a model-dependent measure of proximity, not proof that two passages have the same sociological meaning.

## Chunking {#chunking}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Weeks 3 and 11</span>

**In plain English.** Chunking divides a longer source into smaller units that can be stored, retrieved or sent separately.

```python
transcript_lines = ["opening", "rent increase", "grocery delivery", "meeting", "closing"]
chunks = [transcript_lines[0:2], transcript_lines[2:4], transcript_lines[4:5]]
print(chunks[1])
```

<div class="glossary-output">['grocery delivery', 'meeting']</div>

**Why it matters.** Chunk boundaries can separate a claim from its qualification or a quotation from the interaction that gives it meaning.

## Retrieval, vector search and RAG {#retrieval-rag}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Week 11</span>

**In plain English.** Retrieval selects stored material for a question. Vector search is one possible similarity-based retrieval method. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, places retrieved material into a model request before generation.

<div class="concept-flow"><div><strong>Question</strong><span>what we want to know</span></div><div><strong>Retrieval</strong><span>select source passages</span></div><div><strong>Prompt</strong><span>question plus passages</span></div><div><strong>Generation</strong><span>source-bounded answer</span></div></div>

```python
corpus = {"s01": "Groceries arrived before T01 knew the organizers."}
retrieved_id = "s01"
augmented_prompt = "Use this source only: " + corpus[retrieved_id]
print(augmented_prompt)
```

<div class="glossary-output">Use this source only: Groceries arrived before T01 knew the organizers.</div>

**Why it matters.** RAG can make a source available; it does not guarantee that retrieval found the right source or that the answer represents it accurately.

## Cache {#cache}

<span class="term-meta">Useful · Weeks 1–13</span>

**In plain English.** A cache stores an earlier result so the program can reuse it instead of repeating the same expensive or unavailable operation.

```python
cache = {("score-trust", "text-01"): {"score": 2, "source": "recorded run"}}
result = cache[("score-trust", "text-01")]
print(result)
```

<div class="glossary-output">{'score': 2, 'source': 'recorded run'}</div>

**Why it matters.** Cached output supports teaching and auditing during outages, but it is not a new live run and must be labelled accordingly.
